query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled heat treatment at moderate temperatures (around 500°C) promotes selective oxidation of chromium in the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating to form a thin, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer that acts as a lubricious barrier, thereby enhancing high‐temperature wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate without additional post-deposition treatment
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled vacuum or inert-atmosphere heat treatment at ~500°C for a defined duration to induce optimal Cr-rich oxide formation
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing under sliding or abrasive loads at temperatures in the range of approximately 500–700°C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer on the coating surface
generation.mechanism: Moderate thermal exposure leads to selective oxidation of Cr (relative to Fe, Ni, Co, and Cu) in the coating. The resulting oxide layer provides a hard, self-renewing, and lubricious barrier that limits direct contact between the coating and the counter-surface, thereby reducing abrasive and oxidation wear under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the heat-treated coatings will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate, higher measured surface microhardness, and demonstrate the presence of a continuous Cr-rich oxide layer (identified by techniques such as XPS or SEM) compared to untreated coatings when tested in the 500–700°C temperature range.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating without any post-deposition heat treatment
generation.boundary: Predictions apply within a moderate high-temperature regime (500–700°C) under controlled sliding or abrasion conditions; behavior may differ if temperatures are too low to generate the oxide layer or too high so as to cause excessive degradation of the coating’s mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal treatment duration and atmosphere, the exact composition and thickness of the protective oxide layer, and its long-term stability under cyclic thermal/wear loading remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on a conventional metal substrate. Subject one set to a controlled vacuum or inert-atmosphere heat treatment at approximately 500°C for the optimized duration and leave the other set untreated. Then, perform high-temperature wear tests (in the 500–700°C range) under standardized sliding/abrasive loading conditions.
measurements: Surface oxide layer composition and thickness (using XPS/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the heat-treated coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in wear resistance (lower wear rate), higher microhardness, and demonstrable formation of a continuous Cr-rich oxide layer compared to the untreated baseline under the same testing conditions.

Further investigations have to be conducted to determine the wear behaviour under different wear conditions. The influence of the additional σ-phase has to be investigated in subsequent studies.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Phase Structure and Morphology of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coating
cited_evidence.text: For the room-temperature coating, the high hardness of the coating can resist some abrasive wear and fatigue wear. However, after vacuum heat treatment at 700 °C and 900 °C, due to the decreased hardness of the CS coating, the abrasive wear of the counter-wear ball and quartz sand on the coating surface was intensified, and the crack expansion led to the peeling of the coating.

The wear rates of the two coatings at room temperature are very close. The wear rate for the CS and HVOF coatings reaches its the lowest point after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C. The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of that of the HVOF-500 °C coating. The CS coating with 500 °C vacuum heat treatment has the best wear resistance due to having the highest microhardness. The wear rates and wear amounts of the two coatings heat-treated at 700 °C and 900 °C decreases due to the decrease in microhardness. The wear mechanisms of the CS and HVOF coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.

reading.lever: Use controlled thermal exposure to generate a protective Cr-rich oxide layer in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
reading.why: Prior studies indicate that moderate heat treatments can produce protective oxides and heterogeneous microstructures that enhance wear resistance at elevated temperatures.
